## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

```bash
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

api.c's callback table, ahead of its port waves, in its own file. It is
Settings, a define_ctype! layout with SettingsRef and SettingsMut, kept in
its C layout until port/layout since libgit2's httpclient.c fills one in C;
its typedefs are the aliases SettingsT and HttpParserSettings. Its init
routine, llhttp_settings_init, is Settings::new (and Default), bound with the
type. Each of the 23 slots has a getter returning Option<Callback> or
Option<DataCallback> and a setter taking one.

A slot is set only from batch 1's callable types, whose C half is sound with
any parser, so a table Rust builds is sound with every parser: the handles'
invariant is that every non-NULL slot is such a function, which the getters
rebuild through Callback::from_fn. libgit2's C callbacks read parser->data
as their context, so their table is installed only by C or set_settings_ptr
and reached through its parser's dispatchers; the parser's settings getter
stays the raw address for that reason (callback-context-in-an-argument,
updated with this decision). fld::llhttp__internal_s.settings gains the safe
typed setter ParserMut::set_settings(Option<SettingsRef<'static>>), and
Settings is Send and Sync, so that a static holds one.

The raw bindings gain llhttp_finish and llhttp_reset, which the equivalence
tests call. The ownership store records the slots' pointer findings and
llhttp_settings_init's init role.

4 equiv, 3 doctests, 2 compile-fail doctests.

# A wrap batch ahead of its consumer lists the fields its consumers access

Status: `open`.

## Signal

Skills that contradict each other (`evolution` §2: a defect in the spec). `binding-types`'
Surface section and `scheduling`'s Wrap batches section give a wrap batch that precedes its
consumers the fields *those consumers* access; the `wavefront` tool skill (Scheduling ›
Waves and batches) fills an item's `field_users` from wavefront's `used_fields`, which in a
default schedule are "the fields the closure's own functions access", the type's own
module's functions included (wavefront `docs/batching.md`, Used fields). For a type wrapped
ahead of its consumers, the worklist therefore names fields only the type's own C touches.

## Evidence

`wave-194/batch-0/run-1` (`deps/llhttp/api.c`, wrapping `deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s
`llhttp__internal_s` ahead of api.c's ports). Its `task.json` lists 21 `field_users`, every
field of the struct. `wavefront query structs --name llhttp__internal_s --field-touchers`
shows six of them, `_index`, `_span_pos0`, `_span_cb0`, `_current`, `header_state` and
`initial_message_completed`, touched by `deps/llhttp/llhttp.c`'s functions alone: no
function of api.c, http.c, `transports/httpclient.c` or `transports/httpparser.c` reaches
them. Three of them are unsafe to write from outside the generated parser: `_current` and
`_span_cb0` are the state and span callback it jumps through, `_index` an index into its
match tables. The batch bound the other 15, documented why the six have no accessor, and
filled the dashboard's `fields` cell with the 21 assigned.

## Destination

The spec: the `wavefront` tool skill, Scheduling › Wrap batches, which says how a wrap
batch's items are drawn from the schedule.

## Change

In Scheduling › Wrap batches: a wrap batch ahead of its consumer takes as an item's
`field_users` the fields its consumers access, the item's `used_fields` less those that
only functions of the item's own module touch, as `query structs --field-touchers` lists
them; a field the remaining C of another module touches stays. `binding-types`' Surface
section is unchanged: it already states the rule the worklist then matches.

## Validation

None run: a planning change, validated by the next wrap batch ahead whose type has fields
its own module alone touches, whose `field_users` would hold the 15 consumer fields here.

content.content: --- name: ffibox description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one." --- # ffibox ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a value; what C does not alias is plain Rust. Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md` describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes. What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there. ## Planning ### Dependencies › Adopted crates A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists, each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses. ## Binding workflow ### Binding workflow › Rust tree The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory. ## Binding and porting Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`, `docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too. ### Binding types A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them. ### Binding types › Safe layout While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox;`, and `CArc` for `FooArc`. A value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal`. ### Binding symbols › Functions A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them. ### Binding symbols › Function pointers A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier, `callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body. A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a `CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as `docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox`, its handles unchanged, until its `port/layout` makes it `Box`, or `Pin>` while C keeps its address. Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::() != 0` and `!core::mem::needs_drop::()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its address, `FooBox` is `Box>` and a counted run of them `Vec>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align =`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with `Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions `CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box` and `Vec`. ## Testing ### Testing › UB tests The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test. ## Reviewing Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`. ### Reviewing › Objectives A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`, the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding. ### Reviewing › Reports A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is.

A value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal`. ### Binding symbols › Functions A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them. ### Binding symbols › Function pointers A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier, `callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body. A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a `CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as `docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox`, its handles unchanged, until its `port/layout` makes it `Box`, or `Pin>` while C keeps its address. Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::() != 0` and `!core::mem::needs_drop::()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its address, `FooBox` is `Box>` and a counted run of them `Vec>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align =`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with `Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions `CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box` and `Vec`. ## Testing ### Testing › UB tests The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test. ## Reviewing Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`. ### Reviewing › Objectives A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`, the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding. ### Reviewing › Reports A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is.

# Goals

ffibox is one vocabulary for every value that crosses the boundary between
Rust and a foreign language, in both directions: memory the foreign side
allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust (**inbound**),
and memory Rust owns that the foreign side holds, calls or reads
(**outbound**). The foreign language is C, as G8 states.

Two parties use each primitive:

- a **producer** implements its unsafe internals: a policy, a layout type, a
  seam, an export. A producer may be a human, an agent or a static analysis
  tool;
- a **consumer** uses it through its safe API, without knowing whether C or
  Rust sits behind it.

ffibox is needed only where the foreign side **aliases** a value: keeps a
pointer to it beyond a call, frees it, or shares its refcount or lock. A
pointer passed down for the duration of one call, and memory the foreign side
never sees, are plain Rust: `&mut`, `&`, `Box`, `Vec`, `Arc`.

The goals below are grouped by what they serve. Each states what it means and
how it is checked.

## Familiarity

### G1. Mirror standard Rust

Each primitive mirrors a standard Rust one a Rust programmer already knows:
`CBox` is `Box`, `CArc` is `Arc`, `CVec` is `Vec`, `CGuard` is `MutexGuard`,
`FooRef` / `FooMut` are `&` / `&mut`. Where a foreign convention has no
standard counterpart, it is expressed as the closest composition of standard
idioms rather than a new concept: a lock over part of an object is `Arc<T>`
with a `Mutex` field; a refcount that proves sole ownership is
`Arc::get_mut`.

Where ownership allows it, each primitive converts to and from its standard
counterpart (`Box`, `Vec`, `Arc`, `CStr`, `&[T]`) and implements the standard
traits its counterpart does (`Clone`, `Debug`, `Iterator`, `Eq`, `Hash`), so
that a consumer can leave ffibox as soon as the foreign side stops aliasing.

*Checked by:* every primitive names its standard counterpart in its
documentation, and every departure from it states why.

### G2. No more discipline than standard Rust

A consumer needs no more care with a primitive than with its standard
counterpart: no ordering rules, no manual release, no invariants to remember.
In particular, a consumer writes no `unsafe`.

*Checked by:* consumer code, and the tests of the safe interface, compile with
`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

### G3. Continue ffibox's style

New primitives continue the style ffibox has established: its terms (owner,
handle, policy, seam, adopt, surrender), its naming patterns (`C`-prefixed
owners, `Foo` / `FooRef` / `FooMut` per type, `impl_*!` per policy trait) and
its preference for reusing one primitive across cases over adding one per
case. This is a direction, not a freeze: a new term, name or primitive is
welcome where it is clearer than stretching an existing one, and it states
what it adds and how it relates to the terms beside it.

*Checked by:* the documentation's walk from a foreign declaration to its
wrapper stays a short decision table per direction, and each term it uses is
defined once.

## Expressiveness

### G4. Ownership conventions as Rust idioms

A foreign language's ownership conventions are expressed with Rust's own:
`Drop` for release, `Clone` for copies and reference counts, lifetimes for
borrows and keepalive, `&` / `&mut` exclusivity for access, `Send` / `Sync`
for thread affinity, `Pin` for address sensitivity, `Option` for nullability
and slices for cardinality. A convention that one primitive cannot express is
a gap in the vocabulary, not a reason for a raw pointer in the consumer's API.

*Checked by:* the public interface of a binding carries no raw pointer and no
`unsafe fn` except where an obligation cannot be expressed in types, each
such case documented.

### G5. Foreign patterns as Rust patterns

Beyond ownership, a foreign API follows recurring patterns, and each is
expressed as the standard Rust trait or idiom it corresponds to, declared in
the foreign language's own terms: the producer names the foreign routines and
conventions, and the primitive supplies the Rust side.

| foreign pattern | Rust pattern |
|-----------------|--------------|
| a cursor advanced by `next(it)` until NULL or a status; a `count` and `get(i)` pair; a `->next` chain; a sentinel-terminated array | `Iterator`, `IntoIterator`, slices |
| a `foreach(callback, context)` visitor | a closure, or an `Iterator` where the visit can be suspended |
| a status code, `errno`, an error out-parameter | `Result` with a typed error |
| out-parameters | return values |
| a read or write callback pair over a stream | `Read`, `Write`, `Seek` |
| a key-value option setter, a configuration struct filled before use | a builder |
| a struct of function pointers a library calls into | a trait the Rust side implements |

A pattern is one primitive, parameterised by the routines that implement it,
so that every API using it reads the same in Rust. In the outbound direction,
the same primitive offers a Rust iterator, error or trait to the foreign side
in its own convention.

*Checked by:* the public interface of a binding exposes no foreign pattern
whose Rust counterpart exists: no cursor to advance by hand, no status code to
check, no out-parameter to fill.

### G6. Both directions, symmetrically

Every primitive serves both directions with the same terms. Adopting has
surrendering; a policy that binds a foreign routine has an export that offers
a Rust routine to the foreign side; a foreign callback has a Rust closure
behind a foreign function pointer; a foreign global has a Rust static the
foreign side reads. Either side can produce any ownership shape, and either
can consume it.

*Checked by:* every inbound primitive names its outbound counterpart, or
states why it has none.

### G7. Composable axes

Shape (one object, a run, a string), policy (what release, copy and
construction mean), sharing (sole or counted), lock scope, thread affinity,
address sensitivity and element ownership are independent axes. Primitives
compose along them: owners are elements of vectors, fields of
`#[repr(C)]` structs and contents of guards, with no primitive of their own
for each combination.

*Checked by:* a new combination of axes needs no new primitive.

### G8. C first

ffibox targets C. Its names, the `C`-prefixed owners, `c_drop`, `as_c_ptr`,
are C's, and so are the conventions its primitives encode: `malloc` and
`free`, refcounts, C locks, NUL-terminated strings, status codes and `errno`,
callbacks with a context pointer. No primitive is shaped for a language ffibox
does not serve yet: C++'s move constructors, exceptions and smart pointers,
and Go's pointer-passing rules, are out of scope for now.

When another language is taken on, its conventions are added beside C's
rather than folded into them, and what the two share is factored out then,
from what they actually share, without changing what C bindings write.

*Checked by:* every primitive serves a convention a C API uses.

## Safety

### G9. UB hazards excluded by construction

A binding built from the primitives cannot reach undefined behaviour from safe
code. Each hazard is excluded by a primitive or a producer's contract:

| hazard | excluded by |
|--------|-------------|
| aliasing a foreign object through a reference | handles: no Rust reference over foreign memory that anything may write or free while the reference lives (C, another handle, another thread), and no `&mut` over memory anything else may access |
| moving an address-sensitive object | pinned owners; inline values only for movable layouts |
| null dereference | `NonNull`, `Option` with the null niche |
| invalid values (`_Bool`, `char`, out-of-range enums) | plain-element markers, open enums |
| reading uninitialised memory | `MaybeUninit`, construction phases, `assume_init` |
| misalignment | layout types, alignment bounds on copies |
| out-of-bounds access | slices and runs carrying their length |
| type confusion through erased pointers | typed erasure and recovery |
| use after free, outliving a keepalive | lifetimes, counted references |
| double release, release by the wrong routine | policies pairing release with allocation |
| data races | `Send` / `Sync` opt-in, lock scopes |
| re-entrancy through callbacks | callback arguments typed by the access the caller holds |
| unwinding or `longjmp` across the boundary | panic barriers, documented non-local exits |

Leaks are not undefined behaviour and are not excluded, but no primitive leaks
except by an explicit surrender.

*Checked by:* each hazard has a test that the binding's safe interface cannot
reach it, a compile-fail test where the type system rejects it.

### G10. Safe by default

Every default is the conservative one: foreign types are neither `Send` nor
`Sync`, adopting a pointer is `unsafe`, no status code is discarded, and an
unknown fact selects the more restrictive primitive. Every relaxation is an
explicit opt-in that states its justification.

*Checked by:* a binding with no opt-ins is sound, if less capable.

### G11. Failure semantics

No panic crosses into the foreign language: exports and callbacks have a
barrier that maps a panic to the routine's error convention. No foreign unwind
or `longjmp` crosses Rust frames with destructors. Allocation failure is a
value, `Option` or `Result`, never an abort. Teardown that fails or panics
still releases each object exactly once.

*Checked by:* tests that panic in callbacks, exports and drops, under the
sanitizers.

### G12. Unsafe encapsulated, obligations local

`unsafe` stays with producers, in policy implementations, layout types, seams
and exports, and is crate-private to the binding wherever it can be. Every
unsafe trait and seam states a falsifiable `# Safety` contract in terms of the
foreign side's observable behaviour, checkable one implementation at a time,
without reasoning about the whole program. The distinct obligations are few
and listed, so that auditing a binding is a checklist.

*Checked by:* every `unsafe impl` and `unsafe` block maps to one listed
obligation.

### G13. Type safety through traits

Generic code is bound by traits rather than raw pointers: a policy implements
the lifecycle traits for the exact type it releases, a routine of the wrong
type does not compile, erased values are recovered through the trait of the
type they hold, and a family of foreign types generated from one template or
macro shares one generic wrapper.

*Checked by:* compile-fail tests binding a routine, an element or an erased
value to the wrong type.

### G14. A small, verified trusted base

ffibox's own unsafe code is minimal, and exercised under Miri with strict
provenance, the sanitizers and BorrowSanitizer. Each misuse it claims to
prevent has a compile-fail test. Its guarantees are only as strong as this
base.

*Checked by:* the test suite runs clean under each instrument.

## Cost

### G15. Zero overhead

A primitive costs what the equivalent raw code costs. With a stateless policy
an owner is pointer-sized and a handle is one pointer; runtime state is
carried only when the foreign contract needs it, and no check is made that the
foreign contract does not require.

*Checked by:* compile-time size assertions, and benchmarks against raw calls.

### G16. ABI fidelity

A primitive that stands in for a foreign value has a guaranteed ABI:
`#[repr(transparent)]` where it crosses by value, the null pointer as `None`,
the foreign layout where the foreign side reads its fields.

*Checked by:* compile-time size and alignment assertions against the foreign
layout.

### G17. Stable Rust, `no_std`, no hidden allocation

ffibox builds on stable Rust, with a declared minimum version, and in
`no_std`. It allocates only through a policy or an allocator the consumer
chose. It uses the standard `Allocator` interface where a primitive needs a
non-global allocator. What only nightly Rust can express, such as Rust-defined
variadic functions, is documented as unsupported.

*Checked by:* CI on the minimum supported version, with and without `std`.

## Production

### G18. Producer-agnostic and deterministic

The primitives do not depend on who produces a binding. A binding follows from
facts about each foreign item: ownership and transfer, access, nullability,
cardinality, keepalive, lifecycle role, thread affinity and address
sensitivity. The choice of primitive is a function of those facts, documented
as a table a human reads, an agent follows and a tool implements. A
fact is visible in the binding's types, so that a reviewer or a tool recovers
the facts from the binding. A fact no producer has established selects the
conservative primitive, as G10 describes, so that a partial analysis still
yields a sound binding, and establishing the fact later relaxes it.

*Checked by:* two producers given the same facts emit the same binding.

### G19. Stable through migration

A consumer's code does not change when the producer behind a primitive
changes: a C allocator replaced by Rust's, a C implementation by a Rust
port. Only the policy changes. This is what lets a codebase be ported one module at a time.

*Checked by:* a ported module's consumers compile unchanged against the port.

### G20. Simple macros

Macros mint only what traits and generics cannot: layout types, handles, and
the impls that name a foreign routine. Everything else is ordinary generic
code, provided methods and blanket impls, which the compiler checks and
documents. Each macro does one thing, with a few arms that differ only in
optional trailing parameters; a variant whose expansion differs is a macro of
its own with its own name, as `impl_cdrop_str!` is beside `impl_cdrop!`,
rather than another arm of a larger one. A misuse fails with a type error at
the invocation, not inside the expansion.

*Checked by:* each macro's expansion reads as the impl a producer would write
by hand, and fits on a screen.

## Non-goals

- **Finding the facts.** ffibox records ownership facts in types; it does not
  infer them. Inference is the producer's: a human, an agent or an analysis.
- **Generating bindings.** ffibox is what bindings are written in, not a
  generator. Its regularity serves generators.
- **Memory the foreign side does not alias.** That is standard Rust's.
- **Foreign languages other than C, for now.** See G8.

| aliasing a foreign object through a reference | handles: no Rust reference over foreign memory that anything may write or free while the reference lives (C, another handle, another thread), and no `&mut` over memory anything else may access |
| moving an address-sensitive object | pinned owners; inline values only for movable layouts |
| null dereference | `NonNull`, `Option` with the null niche |
| invalid values (`_Bool`, `char`, out-of-range enums) | plain-element markers, open enums |
| reading uninitialised memory | `MaybeUninit`, construction phases, `assume_init` |
| misalignment | layout types, alignment bounds on copies |
| out-of-bounds access | slices and runs carrying their length |
| type confusion through erased pointers | typed erasure and recovery |
| use after free, outliving a keepalive | lifetimes, counted references |
| double release, release by the wrong routine | policies pairing release with allocation |
| data races | `Send` / `Sync` opt-in, lock scopes |
| re-entrancy through callbacks | callback arguments typed by the access the caller holds |
| unwinding or `longjmp` across the boundary | panic barriers, documented non-local exits |

Leaks are not undefined behaviour and are not excluded, but no primitive leaks
except by an explicit surrender.

*Checked by:* each hazard has a test that the binding's safe interface cannot
reach it, a compile-fail test where the type system rejects it.

### G10. Safe by default

Every default is the conservative one: foreign types are neither `Send` nor
`Sync`, adopting a pointer is `unsafe`, no status code is discarded, and an
unknown fact selects the more restrictive primitive. Every relaxation is an
explicit opt-in that states its justification.

*Checked by:* a binding with no opt-ins is sound, if less capable.

### G11. Failure semantics

No panic crosses into the foreign language: exports and callbacks have a
barrier that maps a panic to the routine's error convention. No foreign unwind
or `longjmp` crosses Rust frames with destructors. Allocation failure is a
value, `Option` or `Result`, never an abort. Teardown that fails or panics
still releases each object exactly once.

*Checked by:* tests that panic in callbacks, exports and drops, under the
sanitizers.

### G12. Unsafe encapsulated, obligations local

`unsafe` stays with producers, in policy implementations, layout types, seams
and exports, and is crate-private to the binding wherever it can be. Every
unsafe trait and seam states a falsifiable `# Safety` contract in terms of the
foreign side's observable behaviour, checkable one implementation at a time,
without reasoning about the whole program. The distinct obligations are few
and listed, so that auditing a binding is a checklist.

*Checked by:* every `unsafe impl` and `unsafe` block maps to one listed
obligation.

### G13. Type safety through traits

Generic code is bound by traits rather than raw pointers: a policy implements
the lifecycle traits for the exact type it releases, a routine of the wrong
type does not compile, erased values are recovered through the trait of the
type they hold, and a family of foreign types generated from one template or
macro shares one generic wrapper.

*Checked by:* compile-fail tests binding a routine, an element or an erased
value to the wrong type.

### G14. A small, verified trusted base

ffibox's own unsafe code is minimal, and exercised under Miri with strict
provenance, the sanitizers and BorrowSanitizer. Each misuse it claims to
prevent has a compile-fail test. Its guarantees are only as strong as this
base.

*Checked by:* the test suite runs clean under each instrument.

## Cost

### G15. Zero overhead

A primitive costs what the equivalent raw code costs. With a stateless policy
an owner is pointer-sized and a handle is one pointer; runtime state is
carried only when the foreign contract needs it, and no check is made that the
foreign contract does not require.

*Checked by:* compile-time size assertions, and benchmarks against raw calls.

### G16. ABI fidelity

A primitive that stands in for a foreign value has a guaranteed ABI:
`#[repr(transparent)]` where it crosses by value, the null pointer as `None`,
the foreign layout where the foreign side reads its fields.

*Checked by:* compile-time size and alignment assertions against the foreign
layout.

### G17. Stable Rust, `no_std`, no hidden allocation

ffibox builds on stable Rust, with a declared minimum version, and in
`no_std`. It allocates only through a policy or an allocator the consumer
chose. It uses the standard `Allocator` interface where a primitive needs a
non-global allocator. What only nightly Rust can express, such as Rust-defined
variadic functions, is documented as unsupported.

*Checked by:* CI on the minimum supported version, with and without `std`.

## Production

### G18. Producer-agnostic and deterministic

The primitives do not depend on who produces a binding. A binding follows from
facts about each foreign item: ownership and transfer, access, nullability,
cardinality, keepalive, lifecycle role, thread affinity and address
sensitivity. The choice of primitive is a function of those facts, documented
as a table a human reads, an agent follows and a tool implements. A
fact is visible in the binding's types, so that a reviewer or a tool recovers
the facts from the binding. A fact no producer has established selects the
conservative primitive, as G10 describes, so that a partial analysis still
yields a sound binding, and establishing the fact later relaxes it.

*Checked by:* two producers given the same facts emit the same binding.

### G19. Stable through migration

A consumer's code does not change when the producer behind a primitive
changes: a C allocator replaced by Rust's, a C implementation by a Rust
port. Only the policy changes. This is what lets a codebase be ported one module at a time.

*Checked by:* a ported module's consumers compile unchanged against the port.

### G20. Simple macros

Macros mint only what traits and generics cannot: layout types, handles, and
the impls that name a foreign routine. Everything else is ordinary generic
code, provided methods and blanket impls, which the compiler checks and
documents. Each macro does one thing, with a few arms that differ only in
optional trailing parameters; a variant whose expansion differs is a macro of
its own with its own name, as `impl_cdrop_str!` is beside `impl_cdrop!`,
rather than another arm of a larger one. A misuse fails with a type error at
the invocation, not inside the expansion.

*Checked by:* each macro's expansion reads as the impl a producer would write
by hand, and fits on a screen.

## Non-goals

- **Finding the facts.** ffibox records ownership facts in types; it does not
  infer them. Inference is the producer's: a human, an agent or an analysis.
- **Generating bindings.** ffibox is what bindings are written in, not a
  generator. Its regularity serves generators.
- **Memory the foreign side does not alias.** That is standard Rust's.
- **Foreign languages other than C, for now.** See G8.

# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.

### `libgit2/src/util/utf8.c` integration: the switch from C

The campaign's first switch, run by `modules/libgit2/src/util/utf8.c/integration/run-1` on the
module's branch after the merge of the working branch (`43605086f`): `012d1d34c`, and the
fork's `1b37e3d08`. The export feature `ffi-export-src-util-utf8-c` is deleted, the crate's
only one, so `utf8.rs`'s gateway compiles from now on, and its four `unit_priv` tests run in
`lib`. The module's six `equiv` tests are retired with the C they compared
(`tests/equiv/src/util/utf8.rs`); their cases stay in its unit tests and doctests. The raw
bindings of `git_utf8_iterate`, `git_utf8_char_length` and `git_utf8_valid_buf_length` stay,
and now reach the exports. `src/util/utf8.c` leaves `c/`: the change is the commit
`integrate src/util/utf8.c` on a local `fork/main`, which stands for
`crustify-rs/libgit2-fork`'s `main` and is not pushed, and `.gitmodules` names the fork.
`utf8.h` stays for `path.c`, `diff_xdiff.c` and `fs_path.c`. The module's tied C test,
`tests/util/utf8.c`, calls `git_utf8_char_length` alone, so it stays and checks the export.
No C test leaves, so no case needs listing. The exports are a private module's, so the
crate's API does not change.

The switch also made the one-time change of the C build. The fork's
`cmake/SelectRust.cmake` links the static library that `LIBGIT2_RUST_LIBRARY` names wherever
the remaining C is linked: `libgit2.so`, the CLI, `libgit2_tests` and `util_tests`. It is an
imported target among `LIBGIT2_SYSTEM_LIBS`. `libgit2.so` keeps the Rust's symbols local
(`--exclude-libs`). Its dynamic symbols are the previous generation's on every variant,
`asan-ubsan`'s two linker-made `__start_`/`__stop_asan_globals` aside. Those come from LLVM
23's instrumentation of the Rust and are protected. Without the variable, the library leaves
the three exports undefined, as the crate's bundled and shared builds of `c/` need. Each
variant's `build` command first makes the library (`crustify/scripts/rust-staticlib.sh`),
between `configure` and the C's link. It builds the crate of the checkout that runs it as a
`staticlib` on the dev profile, the profile the Rust tests run on, so that the C tests check
the same build with debug assertions and overflow checks on. It builds in campaign mode
against the configured variant, with `--features bindgen`, so that the committed bindings
are checked, and with `CRUSTIFY_STATICLIB`, under which `build.rs` reads the build's
configuration and links none of its C. It instruments the Rust as `cargo-variant.sh` does.
`nm` shows that the library defines only the Rust, the three exports and the crate's
`__extern` wrappers, and no libgit2 C. Every other campaign build leaves the library out of
its link, matched by canonical path, so that no binary holds the Rust twice. BSan has no
`cargo bsan rustc`, so a stand-in for the cargo it runs turns its `build` into `rustc
--crate-type staticlib`. The BSan runtime its driver bundles is removed from the copy, since
the variant's C link links it.

configured from the generation's own `c`, a detached worktree of the fork at `1b37e3d08`, so
that the build outlives this worktree and the base checkout's next moves (`build.json`
version 7). Each archive holds 212 objects, where the previous generation's held 213:
`utf8.c.o` is gone. Each variant passed its smoke test (`util_tests -sutf8`). In every
variant, `utf8proc_utf8class` is absent from the C test executables, which take

#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.

# A callback whose context is reached through an argument has no sound C form

Status: `open` (weighed by `wave-194/batch-2/run-1`; the spec change is not made).

## Signal

Skills that leave a case unspecified that a binding cannot settle well (`evolution` §2).
`binding-symbols`' Function pointers section builds a callable type's C half from "a C
function, with its context, which Rust calls … through an `unsafe` constructor whose
contract states … its context's lifetime and threads, and safe to call". For a function
pointer "without a context parameter" it says the Rust half carries no captured state. It
does not cover the case where C has no context parameter because the context lives in an
argument: there the C function's soundness depends on the argument, not on anything the
callable type holds, so a safe `call` with an arbitrary argument cannot be sound.

## Evidence

`wave-194/batch-1/run-1`: `llhttp_cb` (`int (*)(llhttp_t *)`) and `llhttp_data_cb` take no
context; their context is the parser's `data`, which libgit2's C callbacks
(`transports/httpclient.c`'s `on_header_field`, `on_body`, …) read as an
`http_parser_context *`. The batch's `Callback::from_fn` (`pub(crate)`) can only require
that the function be sound "with every live, exclusively held parser, whatever its `data`
and `settings` hold", which no such C callback meets: `Callback::call(Parser::new()…)`
would hand it a NULL `data`. The sound C form is the call made through the settings its
parser executes with, whose contract (`set_settings_ptr`) vouches for that parser; the
batch leaves that to the settings binding (api.c's `wrap`).

## Destination

The spec: `binding-symbols`, Function pointers, its three cases that shape the type.

## Change

Not made yet. `wave-194/batch-2/run-1`, the next batch that binds the table holding such
callbacks, weighed the two candidates and took the first, which needs no new primitive:

- the callable type's C half keeps the strong contract, sound with any argument whatever
  context it carries, and a C function that reads its context from an argument is never
  one, so `call` stays safe;
- a table of callables, bound as a layout whose slots are set only from the callable types,
  is sound with any object, and the object's setter that stores it is safe, taking a
  `'static` borrow where C keeps its address (`ParserMut::set_settings(Option<&'static
  Settings>)`);
- a table C builds of functions that read their context from the object is stored only
  through the object's `unsafe` setter, whose contract vouches for the object's context
  (`set_settings_ptr`), and is read back from the object as the address it holds, not as the
  table's handle, whose getters would hand out callables callable with any object; its
  functions are reached only through the routine of the object that dispatches them (api.c's
  `CALLBACK_MAYBE`, `port` in wave 195), with that object.

In `binding-symbols` § Function pointers, as a fourth case after "one without a context
parameter carries no captured state":

> - one whose context C reaches through another argument, such as the object it is
>   handed, has a C half only for functions sound with any such argument. A C function
>   that reads its context there is reached only through the object that holds it, by the
>   routine that dispatches it with that object, never as the callable type: a field or
>   table that holds such functions is set from C, or through an `unsafe` setter whose
>   contract carries the object's context, and read back as no callable.

## Evidence (`wave-194/batch-2/run-1`)

`llhttp_settings_s`, bound as `Settings` in `src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.rs`: its 23 slots
are set from `Callback` / `DataCallback` only, read back as them through the handles'
invariant (each non-NULL slot is one `from_fn` accepts), and `Settings` is `Send` and
`Sync`, so that a `static` holds one, as libgit2's `httpclient.c` does in C. `ParserRef`'s
`settings` getter stays the raw address: `transports/httpclient.c`'s `on_header_field`,
`on_body` and the others cast `parser->data` to `http_parser_context *`, so a
`SettingsRef` over that table would let `Settings`' getter return a `DataCallback` whose
safe `call(Parser::new().as_mut(), …)` hands them a NULL context.

## Validation

None run.

## Review

None yet.
